title: Mathematics, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade
answer: A team of researchers spent months designing an AI math tutor for fifth graders. It followed a strict set of rules: first figure out where the student was stuck, then choose what kind of help to give, then respond only in ways that fit that choice.

papers.why: Concrete design for a guardrailed primary math tutor; supports testing in real classrooms, not just simulations.
papers.title: Taming the black box: Design principles for rule-integrated LLM tutoring systems in primary school mathematical problem solving
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Rule-guided LLM math tutor for primary word problems: diagnosis, then intent selection, then constrained response. Simulations and a pilot with 40 Grade 5 students showed more consistent scaffolding, fewer premature answers, and sustained engagement. Classroom pilot surfaced fragmented inputs and attention swings missed in simulation.

papers.title: A systematic review of the impact of GenAI on learning performance, AI hallucinations, and problem-solving in computer science education
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Systematic review of GenAI in CS education: performance, hallucinations, problem solving.

papers.why: Performance is not learning. Students prefer the tool that helps them less.
papers.title: Less stress, better scores, same learning: The dissociation of performance and learning in AI-supported programming education
papers.caveat: University CS1 course (N=275), single 90-minute exercise; two-item cognitive load subscales had limited reliability per authors.
papers.finding: RCT (N=275, university CS1). Both a hint-first tutor and ChatGPT raised exercise scores but neither raised learning; only the hint-first tutor raised intrinsic motivation. Students preferred ChatGPT.

papers.why: Dosage finding is useful if it holds.
papers.title: Enhancing Learning Outcomes through AI-Based Tutoring Systems: A Study on Student Motivation and Academic Achievement
papers.venue: ACADEMIA International Journal for Social Sciences
papers.caveat: Low-profile journal; results not independently verified. This is not verified.
papers.finding: Reported randomized trial (N=602, grades 7-10): adaptive tutoring raised achievement (d about 0.40), more for low-baseline students, gains leveled after about 12 hours.

papers.title: A systematic review of AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) in K-12 education
papers.caveat: Review quality depends on included studies.
papers.finding: 28 quasi-experimental K-12 studies, 4,597 students: intelligent tutoring effects generally positive but smaller when compared with non-intelligent tutoring systems.

papers.why: Realistic effect size for K-12 math AI to set expectations.
papers.title: The Effectiveness of AI on K-12 Students’ Mathematics Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.venue: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education
papers.finding: Meta-analysis of 21 K-12 math studies: small positive effect of AI (0.34), larger for intelligent tutoring and adaptive systems.

papers.title: The use of a personalized learning approach to implementing self-regulated online learning
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Quasi-experiment in secondary physics: personalized learning paths within self-regulated online learning raised post-test and learning gains over conventional online learning.

papers.title: Adaptive formative assessment system based on computerized adaptive testing and the learning memory cycle for personalized learning
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Adaptive formative assessment combining computerized adaptive testing with memory-cycle review beat CAT alone and non-adaptive tests in a 7-week university programming course.

papers.why: Supports adaptive hints that keep challenge right-sized.
papers.title: AI-Induced guidance: Preserving the optimal Zone of Proximal Development
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Discovery-learning game where AI adapted instruction text in real time kept learners in their zone of proximal development: higher learning, lower cognitive load, same enjoyment versus static instructions.

papers.why: Background for the adaptive practice theme; reinforces the prototype-to-practice gap.
papers.title: AI-enabled adaptive learning systems: A systematic mapping of the literature
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Mapping, not effect evaluation; mostly higher ed.
papers.finding: Mapping of 147 studies (2014-2020) on AI-enabled adaptive learning. Identifies intervention types and common analytic techniques, and notes few systems are actually implemented to address real student problems.

children.name: Adaptive Practice With Regrouping
children.blurb: Adaptive practice with regrouping is the use of AI math programs that adjust each problem to a student's last answer, paired with a teacher who uses the program's reports to form next-day small groups.

children.name: Hints, Not Answers
children.blurb: Hints, not answers means configuring a general AI tool so it guides a student through a math problem instead of solving it for them.

children.name: Practice With AI, Checks Without It
children.blurb: Practice with AI, checks without it is a routine in which students use an AI tool for most of their practice and then sit a short assessment with no tool available, so the teacher can compare the two results.

children.name: Sorting Misconceptions From Student Work
children.blurb: Sorting misconceptions from student work means using an approved AI tool to group wrong math answers by the kind of mistake they reveal, so a teacher can see which misunderstandings are common across a class instead of reading every paper alone.

children.name: Word Problems, Warm Ups, and Retake Forms
children.blurb: This idea is using AI to generate math word problems, warm up review problems, and parallel retake forms.

children.name: Visual Models and Real Data
children.blurb: Visual Models and Real Data is the idea that students grasp mathematics more firmly when the mathematics is something they can see and handle, through graphing tools, data they collect themselves, and simulations built around real prices.

children.name: Feedback on Reasoning and Proofs
children.blurb: Feedback on reasoning and proofs means using a school configured AI tutor to comment on the logic of a student's mathematical explanation, not to supply the answer or write the proof.

children.name: Support for Tutors and Intervention Groups
children.blurb: This idea is about using AI to support the adults who teach math, especially tutors and teachers running intervention groups, rather than having AI teach students directly.

children.name: Students With Disabilities and English Learners
children.blurb: This idea is about using AI practice tools to support students with disabilities and English learners in kindergarten through 12th grade mathematics.

children.name: When Students May Use AI in Math
children.blurb: When students may use AI in math is a decision a teacher makes for each task, in the same way math teachers have long set their own rules for calculators.

children.name: Algebra Readiness and Placement
children.blurb: Algebra readiness and placement is the decision about when a student takes algebra and which math courses follow.

children.name: Catching the Machine's Mistakes
children.blurb: Catching the machine's mistakes is a math activity where students review AI solutions to problems they have already learned, some correct and some wrong, and explain the errors.

children.name: Helping Families Help at Home
children.blurb: Helping Families Help at Home is a practice where teachers use AI to create short, clear guides about the math methods used in class, then send them home in the family's language.

children.name: Planning Math Units With AI
children.blurb: Planning math units with AI means a teacher asks an approved tool for a first draft of a unit, such as a lesson sequence and a list of common misconceptions, and then reshapes it to fit the class and the district's curriculum.

sections.body: Mathematics from kindergarten through twelfth grade is a part of school life where students practice procedures, build understanding, and work through problems, and the book describes AI helping with adaptive practice, hints, and the endless supply of problems teachers need. It also covers hint only tutors, the rhythm of practice and checks done without AI, misconception sorting, problem writing, visual models and real data, feedback on reasoning, support for tutors, readiness flags, and guides for families. The book warns that AI can quietly undermine learning when it hands out answers, and it can make arithmetic mistakes while sounding completely sure. The teacher's judgment is what turns the tool into a help rather than a shortcut. Figure 7.2 maps these ideas to grade bands and evidence, with three carrying strong evidence and the rest sensible practices that should start as small pilots.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that AI can help a great deal in math, especially with adaptive practice, hints, and the endless supply of problems, and the chapter's opening study, Taming the black box, shows a rule guided tutor gave more consistent support and fewer premature answers than an unguided chatbot. It also finds that simulations missed how real students type half sentences, jump between ideas, and lose focus, so real classrooms are messier than any model of them. What does not work is the answer machine in disguise, where practice scores climb and everyone assumes learning is rising while nobody tests whether the tool gives answers or checks performance without it. The rule the book holds to is that the teacher's judgment turns the tool into a help rather than a shortcut, and the honest answer needs results from work done without the tool. The Thirty Day Move is to ask every AI math tool to solve a problem outright, reconfigure any tool that gives the full answer using Figure 7.3 or limit it to teacher use, and start the weekly rhythm in Figure 7.4 with a short paper quiz each Friday to compare practice and quiz scores after a month.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A teacher would start with Adaptive Practice With Regrouping and Hints, Not Answers for daily practice, then use Practice With AI, Checks Without It to keep the weekly rhythm honest. For diagnosing student work, Sorting Misconceptions From Student Work and Word Problems, Warm Ups, and Retake Forms help turn errors into next steps, while Visual Models and Real Data and Feedback on Reasoning and Proofs support deeper math thinking. Leaders can use Support for Tutors and Intervention Groups, Students With Disabilities and English Learners, and When Students May Use AI in Math to set support and boundaries, and Algebra Readiness and Placement for readiness flags. Catching the Machine's Mistakes belongs with any tool use, Helping Families Help at Home gives parents a clear role, and Planning Math Units With AI ties the chapter together for unit design. A parent would go to Helping Families Help at Home for ways to support without giving answers, and a leader would go to Planning Math Units With AI for the board question and evidence.
